evals.prompt: I run engineering at Meridian Freight Cloud, a logistics SaaS. About 400 customer dev teams build against our public shipment-tracking API and we want that to become a real business line, so I opened a req for a Senior Platform Engineer six weeks ago. Our recruiter sponsored a booth at PlatformCon and has been posting in the Backstage community Slack every week. We've had 31 applicants and every single one wants to talk about Kubernetes operators, Argo CD and internal golden paths. Nobody has ever shipped anything a customer integrates against. Where should we actually be fishing, and what do I change?
evals.expected_output: Establishes that the role's consumer is external developers, classifies it as an external-API platform hire rather than internal developer platform work, explains that PlatformCon and Backstage serve the internal-IDP population, and redirects sourcing to apidays plus general senior-backend-engineering channels with open-source contribution history as a screen.
expectations: Asks or states explicitly whether the primary consumer of what this role builds is the company's own engineering teams or developers outside the company
Classifies the role as an external/public-API platform hire rather than internal developer platform (IDP) work
Identifies PlatformCon as serving the internal-developer-platform audience rather than this role's audience
Identifies the Backstage community as an internal-IDP channel and therefore the wrong applicant pool for this hire
Recommends apidays as a sourcing venue for API platform engineers
States that apidays names API platform engineers and API product managers among its stated audience
Recommends general senior-backend-engineering sourcing channels such as referral networks and senior-IC pipelines for this track
Names open-source contribution history as a screening signal reviewable as existing evidence rather than tested live
Does not recommend DevRel-adjacent channels (developer-advocate job boards, DevRel Slack or Discord, conference speaker circuits) as the primary pool for this role
States that the posting itself must say explicitly whether the role means internal-IDP or external-API platform engineering
Attributes the six weeks of irrelevant applicants to a channel and audience mismatch rather than only to compensation or job-title wording

evals.prompt: Calder Analytics here, 60 people, B2B analytics product that's been selling for seven years. Four months ago we shipped a public REST API because three enterprise accounts demanded it. Right now two backend engineers keep it alive on top of their normal roadmap work. Our CEO wants to get serious about it and has signed off budget for three hires starting in Q1: an API Product Manager, a Platform Architect, and a Partner Engineer. Can you write me the three scorecards so I can hand them to the recruiter on Monday?
evals.expected_output: Classifies the company as the bolt-on public API archetype, cites the 84% small-teams finding, pushes back on the three-role split as oversized for a two-person API surface, and only produces scorecards that name the archetype, the measured metric, and quantified outcomes.
expectations: Classifies Calder Analytics as the bolt-on public API archetype rather than infra/API-first or enterprise partner ecosystem
Cites Postman's finding that 84% of API teams operate in groups of 1-9 people
Pushes back on hiring three specialized roles at once and recommends sizing the hire to the current two-person API surface
States that at a bolt-on company API design is typically one line item inside a general backend-engineering role rather than a dedicated platform team's sole mandate
Notes that splitting API PM, platform architect and partner engineer into three separate people is the exception rather than the norm
Asks or establishes how many people currently own the API surface end to end before producing any scorecard
Frames a first dedicated platform hire at this company as a real resourcing shift rather than a routine backfill
Does not apply the infra/API-first bar (staff level, 12+ years, prior leadership of API-design teams) as the bar for this company
Any scorecard produced names the company archetype and the specific metric the role is measured on
Any scorecard produced lists quantified outcomes rather than vague responsibilities such as owning the platform

evals.prompt: Draft req for Nimbus Ledger (Series B fintech), about to go live. Title: Senior API Platform Engineer. Responsibilities: design and ship our v2 public payments API; own the integration architecture for 12 named partner integrations in year one; write the developer blog and run quarterly community office hours; grow monthly active API keys by 40%. Reports to: TBD. Team: solo for now, we'll see how it goes. Comp band already agreed. Does this look hireable? Tighten it up for me and I'll post it this afternoon.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to approve the posting, names the build-plus-outreach scope collapse and the three-function outcome stack, flags the missing reporting line and headcount plan, distinguishes the pattern from DevRel's gatekeeper taxonomy, states plainly that no named sourced taxonomy exists here, and recommends splitting the scope or stating the resourcing explicitly.
expectations: Flags the posting as a scope-collapse red flag rather than approving it as hireable
Names the stacking of build work (API design, partner-integration architecture) with outreach work (developer blog, community office hours) as the specific pattern
Notes the posting carries outcomes belonging to three different functions: a shipped API surface, a named partner-integration count, and a content, community or usage metric
Flags the absence of any stated headcount plan for eventually splitting the scope
Flags the missing reporting line and the absent budget for growing the function past one person
States that the failure here is execution volume across multiple full-time jobs rather than an impossible-skills list
Distinguishes this pattern from DevRel's gatekeeper/pit-trap taxonomy rather than relabeling that taxonomy
States plainly that no named, sourced hiring-red-flag taxonomy exists for developer-platform roles and presents this diagnosis as a structural inference rather than a quoted industry framework
Names the mismatch between the IC-engineering seniority the title implies and responsibilities that read as a product manager's job plus a DevRel job layered on top
Recommends either splitting the scope across more than one hire or stating the resourcing explicitly in the posting before it goes out
Recommends the posting state explicitly that this is external-API platform engineering rather than internal developer platform work

evals.prompt: Trellis Comms, CPaaS company, our messaging API basically is the product. 140 engineers. We're hiring a Staff Platform Engineer to own the public API surface. We already run a standard loop for senior backend: one 60-minute system design round (the usual prompts, design a URL shortener or design Twitter), two coding rounds, one behavioral. I was planning to just reuse it. Sanity-check me and tell me what to add. Constraint: I can't spend more than 5 interviewer-hours per candidate total, and we do have a recruiter doing the first call.
evals.expected_output: Adds an API-design round distinct from general system design, describes what it judges and how its scope differs, gives a developer-as-user prompt, sets the infra/API-first bar, fits the 5-hour ceiling by deleting stages, and declines to present any company's posted loop as an industry standard.
expectations: Recommends adding an API-design round that is distinct from the general system-design round
States that API design and system design are two separate named interview formats used at major companies
States the API-design round is judged on developer-facing usability and resistance to misuse rather than raw scale trade-offs
Names clarity, predictability, being hard to misuse, or error messages specific enough for a developer to act on, as the bar for the API-design round
Notes the API-design round's scope is deliberately smaller than full system design, with no full architecture to sketch
Offers a concrete API-design prompt whose users are developers integrating the API, such as a card-payment-processing API
Classifies Trellis Comms as the infra/API-first archetype where the API is the product and sets the highest technical-depth bar accordingly
Respects the 5-interviewer-hour ceiling by deleting loop stages rather than only reordering or shortening them
Does not present any named company's posted loop as a universal industry standard
States that no single fully documented developer-platform-specific loop is published for every track and presents the resulting loop as an assembled design

evals.prompt: Hollis Retail Systems, enterprise retail platform. Roughly 1,200 ISV partners build on our partner API and that ecosystem is where our growth is coming from. We're hiring our first API Product Manager. Head of Product wants to run our standard engineering loop on them: a 45-minute Python coding screen, then a system design round, then two behavioral interviews. No hard deadline, and this will probably be the first of three platform hires over the next year so I want whatever we build to be reusable. Give me the loop, what each stage tests, and the outcomes I should put on the scorecard.
evals.expected_output: Drops the coding screen for the PM track, weights a scoping and design-thinking round, allows a no-code technical conversation, cites the PM-loop precedent, classifies the enterprise partner-ecosystem archetype, names partner-facing outcome metrics, and builds the loop as a reusable artefact.
expectations: Removes or replaces the Python coding screen for the API Product Manager track
Recommends a scoping and design-thinking round weighted over a coding round
States the PM candidate is assessed on how they scope, structure and communicate design thinking rather than on proving deep technical implementation expertise
Allows a technical conversation in which the PM explains APIs and how a system fits together without writing code
Cites Google's or Uber's own PM loop practice as the precedent for that weighting
Recommends a written product exercise only if the company's general PM process already uses one
Classifies Hollis Retail Systems as the enterprise partner-ecosystem archetype
Names partner-facing outcome metrics such as partners supported, integrations shipped or launched, integration usage, or year-over-year growth, rather than a generic own-the-API outcome
Builds the loop as a reusable artefact because this is the first of several hires rather than a one-off

evals.prompt: Varnhold Systems, 300-person B2B SaaS. I need a number for the req today. Our recruiter pulled Glassdoor and Levels.fyi for 'platform engineer' and got $155k-$210k base, then averaged in postings for 'API developer' and 'integration engineer' to widen the sample size. We're leveling this person as our L5, same as our other senior backend folks. Just give me the offer range to put in the requisition and the one-line justification I can send the CFO.
evals.expected_output: Refuses the blended crowdsourced figure as market rate, anchors the offer to the company's own general engineering ladder at L5, explains why bespoke title searches return sparse data, cites Stripe's general-ladder title as one sourced example, and requires any figure to carry source, date and level.
expectations: Refuses to present the $155k-$210k crowdsourced range as a verified market rate
Rejects blending platform engineer, API developer and integration engineer postings into a single averaged range
Anchors the offer to the company's own general software-engineering ladder at the L5-equivalent level
States that bespoke platform engineer or API product manager title searches return sparse crowdsourced data
Cites Stripe's Staff Software Engineer, API Platform title as evidence that the leveling word is a general-ladder rung with the platform name as a team qualifier
Presents that company example as one sourced data point rather than a universal industry standard
Requires any figure used to carry its source, date and level, and never an undated number quoted from memory
Recommends searching crowdsourced leveling data by the general engineering title plus team name rather than by the bespoke platform title
Gives the general-ladder anchor as the actionable answer rather than hedging the compensation question away as unanswerable

evals.prompt: Okabe Cloud, Series A. I need to hire a Developer Platform Engineer and I want your help with the scorecard and the interview loop. The job: run our developer community Discord, write tutorials and sample apps for our API, speak at about three conferences a year, and collect feedback from integrators to bring back to the product team. Budget is one headcount. What should the loop look like?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the responsibilities as a developer-relations role despite the platform title, routes the user to the DevRel hiring skill, explains the screening difference, declines to build an API-design round, and flags the title-versus-responsibilities mismatch.
expectations: Identifies the described responsibilities as a developer-relations or advocacy role rather than a developer-platform engineering role
Routes the user to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-hiring
States that DevRel roles are screened primarily on communication and community craft while developer-platform roles are screened on API and system design judgment
Does not produce an API-design interview round for this role
Flags the mismatch between the platform engineering title and the responsibilities, and recommends retitling or splitting the role rather than hiring under the platform title as written
